claims.claim: Increased acetylcholine levels in ace-1;ace-2 mutants result in precocious elevation of spine density during development.
claims.source: In contrast, increased acetylcholine levels (i.e., in ace-1;ace-2 mutants) results in precocious elevation of spine density during development (Figure 5D and E and S4C).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by quantitative measurements of spine density in ace-1;ace-2 double mutants.

claims.claim: The developmental elevation of spine density is blocked in unc-31/CAPS mutants.
claims.source: The developmental elevation of spine density is also blocked in unc-31/CAPS mutants (Speese et al., 2007), in which neuropeptide and catecholamine neurotransmitter release is also prevented (Figure 5—figure supplement 1D and E).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by quantitative measurements of spine density in unc-31 mutants and cites previous work characterizing this mutant.

claims.claim: Animals grown in the presence of histamine to silence cholinergic neurons show reduced spine density at the L4 stage.
claims.source: Animals grown in the presence of histamine showed reduced spine density at the L4 stage compared to animals grown on plates without histamine (Figure 5F–I).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by experiments using histamine-gated chloride channels to reduce cholinergic activity.

claims.claim: Optogenetic activation of A-class motor neurons during L2-L3 development leads to increased spine density in L3 larvae.
claims.source: Animals were exposed to 561 nm light to activate ceChrimson for a brief period (1 s every 4 s) during the L2-L3 stage larval development (See Materials and methods). This treatment led to increased spine density (scored in L3 larvae) in comparison to animals without ceChrimson stimulation (Figure 5J–M).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by optogenetic experiments showing that temporal activation of cholinergic neurons increases spine density.

claims.claim: VD-class GABAergic neurons display dendritic spines throughout the dorsal nerve cord.
claims.source: This experiment confirmed the presence of dendritic spines in VD neurons throughout the dorsal nerve cord (Figure 5—figure supplement 2A-D).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by Airyscan imaging of VD neurons after DD ablation.

claims.claim: EM reconstruction of 27 μm of the anterior VD2 dendrite detected nine dendritic spines.
claims.source: Our EM reconstruction of 27 μm of the anterior VD2 dendrite detected nine dendritic spines (Figure 4—figure supplement 1E).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by EM reconstruction data.

claims.claim: Most VD spines are juxtaposed to presynaptic termini of cholinergic motor neurons (DA2, DB1, AS2).
claims.source: Similar to DD1, most VD spines are juxtaposed to presynaptic termini of cholinergic motor neurons (DA2, DB1, AS2).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by EM reconstruction data showing VD spine contacts with cholinergic presynaptic termini.

claims.claim: Dendritic spines were originally described by Ramon y Cajal.
claims.source: These dendritic 'spines' were originally described by Ramon y Cajal (Yuste, 2015) and are now recognized as key functional components of neural circuits.
claims.evidence: The claim cites a historical reference about the original description of dendritic spines.

claims.claim: Spine morphology and density are regulated by neural activity in plastic responses that are strongly correlated with learning and memory.
claims.source: For example, spine morphology and density are regulated by neural activity in plastic responses that are strongly correlated with learning and memory (Kozorovitskiy et al., 2005; Moser et al., 1997).
claims.evidence: The claim cites previous studies showing correlation between spine plasticity and learning/memory.

claims.claim: Spine-like protrusions have been reported for invertebrate neurons.
claims.source: Although spine-like protrusions have been reported for invertebrate neurons (Leiss, 2008; Petralia et al., 2016), few studies (Bushey et al., 2011; Scott et al., 2003) have rigorously determined if these structures share functional features with vertebrate spines.
claims.evidence: The claim cites previous reports of spine-like structures in invertebrates.

claims.claim: The anatomy of the C. elegans nervous system was originally defined by reconstruction of electron micrographs of serial sections.
claims.source: The anatomy of the C. elegans nervous system was originally defined by reconstruction of electron micrographs (EM) of serial sections. This approach revealed that a small subset of neurons displays short, spine-like protrusions. These include five classes of motor neurons (RMD, RME, SMD, DD, VD) and an interneuron (RIP) (White et al., 1976; White et al., 1986).
claims.evidence: The claim cites the original EM reconstruction studies of the C. elegans nervous system.

claims.claim: Light and electron microscopy detected similar dendritic protrusions extending from motor neurons in the nematode Ascaris.
claims.source: Light and electron microscopy detected similar dendritic protrusions extending from motor neurons in the nematode, Ascaris (Angstadt et al., 1989; Stretton et al., 1978).
claims.evidence: The claim cites previous studies detecting dendritic protrusions in Ascaris.

claims.claim: Recent reports used light microscopy to show that a postsynaptic acetylcholine receptor is localized near the tips of spine-like protrusions on DD class motor neurons that directly appose presynaptic termini.
claims.source: Finally, recent reports used light microscopy to show that a postsynaptic acetylcholine receptor is localized near the tips of spine-like protrusions on the DD class motor neurons that directly appose presynaptic termini (Oliver et al., 2018; Philbrook et al., 2018).
claims.evidence: The claim cites recent studies showing acetylcholine receptor localization at DD spine tips.

claims.claim: The actin cytoskeleton is a structural hallmark of vertebrate dendritic spines.
claims.source: Because the actin cytoskeleton is a structural hallmark of vertebrate dendritic spines (Cingolani and Goda, 2008), we also labeled DD neurons with the actin marker, LifeAct::GFP (Riedl et al., 2008).
claims.evidence: The claim cites established knowledge about actin in vertebrate spines and the source of the LifeAct marker.

claims.claim: EM reconstruction of mammalian dendritic spines in the hippocampus revealed that thin and mushroom shapes predominate.
claims.source: EM reconstruction of mammalian dendritic spines in the hippocampus also revealed that thin and mushroom shapes predominate (Harris and Stevens, 1989; Harris et al., 1992) and that filopodial and stubby spines are less abundant (Fiala et al., 1998; Zuo et al., 2005).
claims.evidence: The claim cites previous EM studies of mammalian spine morphology.

claims.claim: A similarly heterogeneous array of spine shapes among mammalian neurons has been attributed to active remodeling of spine architecture.
claims.source: Although we have assigned DD motor neuron spines to four discrete classifications, both fluorescence imaging and EM reconstruction point to a broader array of spine types that includes potential intermediate forms (Figure 1G–H; 2C). A similarly heterogeneous array of spine shapes among mammalian neurons has been attributed to active remodeling of spine architecture (Sala and Segal, 2014; Zuo et al., 2005).
claims.evidence: The claim cites previous studies attributing heterogeneous spine shapes to active remodeling.

claims.claim: In the mature mammalian cortex, extended imaging has revealed transient filopodial extensions with a lifetime shorter than a day, and potential plasticity over longer intervals, where approximately half of spines are stable for months.
claims.source: In the mature mammalian cortex, extended imaging has revealed transient filopodial extensions with a lifetime shorter than a day, and potential plasticity over longer intervals, where approximately half of spines are stable for months (Trachtenberg et al., 2002; Zuo et al., 2005).
claims.evidence: The claim cites previous studies of spine dynamics in mammalian cortex.

claims.claim: Disruption of the Arp2/3 complex or its activators has been previously shown to reduce dendritic spine density in the mammalian brain and to impair function.
claims.source: Disruption of the Arp2/3 complex or its activators has been previously shown to reduce dendritic spine density in the mammalian brain and to impair function (Kim et al., 2013; Lippi et al., 2011; Soderling et al., 2003; Spence et al., 2016; Westphal et al., 2000).
claims.evidence: The claim cites multiple previous studies showing effects of Arp2/3 disruption on mammalian spine density.

claims.claim: Functional dendritic spines are sites of presynaptic input.
claims.source: Because functional dendritic spines are sites of presynaptic input (Alvarez and Sabatini, 2007; Hering and Sheng, 2001; Petralia et al., 2016), we investigated the disposition of DD spines vis-a-vis their main presynaptic partners, the cholinergic VA and VB class motor neurons (Figure 2A).
claims.evidence: The claim cites established knowledge about dendritic spines being sites of presynaptic input.

claims.claim: Individual spines on GABAergic neurons in the mammalian hippocampus can have inputs from multiple presynaptic termini.
claims.source: We note that individual spines on GABAergic neurons in the mammalian hippocampus can also have inputs from multiple presynaptic termini (Acsády et al., 1998; Gulyás et al., 1992; Petralia et al., 2016).
claims.evidence: The claim cites previous studies showing multiple inputs to individual spines in mammalian hippocampus.

claims.claim: Robustly stained PSDs are observed at vertebrate glutamatergic synapses, but PSDs are either absent or much less prominent in electron micrographs of vertebrate synapses at spines for other neurotransmitters (glycine, GABA, acetylcholine).
claims.source: Although robustly stained PSDs are observed at vertebrate glutamatergic synapses, PSDs are either absent or much less prominent in electron micrographs of vertebrate synapses at spines for other neurotransmitters (glycine, GABA, acetylcholine) (Knott et al., 2002; Kubota et al., 2007; Umbriaco et al., 1994).
claims.evidence: The claim cites previous studies showing differences in PSD staining at different types of vertebrate synapses.

claims.claim: Key cytoplasmic organelles such as Smooth Endoplasmic Reticulum (SER) are present in both dendritic shafts and spines of mammalian neurons.
claims.source: Key cytoplasmic organelles such as Smooth Endoplasmic Reticulum (SER), are present in both dendritic shafts and spines of mammalian neurons (Harris and Stevens, 1989).
claims.evidence: The claim cites previous studies showing SER in mammalian dendritic spines.

claims.claim: Spine SER regulates activity-dependent Ca++ release through the ryanodine receptor.
claims.source: In addition to its role of processing membrane proteins, spine SER regulates activity-dependent Ca++ release through the ryanodine receptor (Fill and Copello, 2002).
claims.evidence: The claim cites previous work on the role of SER in Ca++ release.

claims.claim: Polysomes and rough ER have been reported in spines, consistent with the possibility of local translation at synapses.
claims.source: Other structures such as polysomes and rough ER have also been reported in spines, consistent with the possibility of local translation at synapses (Bourne and Harris, 2008; Hafner et al., 2019; Nimchinsky et al., 2002; Steward and Reeves, 1988).
claims.evidence: The claim cites previous studies reporting polysomes and rough ER in spines.

claims.claim: Mitochondria and microtubules are reported to be rare in the dendritic spines of mature mammalian neurons.
claims.source: Mitochondria and microtubules are reported to be rare in the dendritic spines of mature mammalian neurons (Bourne and Harris, 2008; Nimchinsky et al., 2002).
claims.evidence: The claim cites previous reports about the rarity of mitochondria and microtubules in mammalian spines.

claims.claim: Ca++ is a key signaling molecule to mediate activity-dependent synaptic plasticity.
claims.source: Ca++ is a key signaling molecule to mediate activity-dependent synaptic plasticity (Lee et al., 2016; Rochefort and Konnerth, 2012).
claims.evidence: The claim cites established knowledge about the role of Ca++ in synaptic plasticity.

claims.claim: Muscle cells that share cholinergic input with DD spines display prolonged elevation of Ca++ over a period of seconds.
claims.source: Muscle cells that share cholinergic input with DD spines also display prolonged elevation of Ca++ over a period of seconds (Liu et al., 2013), suggesting that cholinergic neurons regulate the long lasting bursts of Ca++ in spines and muscle cells.
claims.evidence: The claim cites a previous study showing Ca++ dynamics in muscle cells receiving cholinergic input.

claims.claim: A similar explanation of convergent input was proposed for the coordinated firing of adjacent dendritic spines in rat hippocampal neurons.
claims.source: A similar explanation of convergent input was proposed for the coordinated firing of adjacent dendritic spines in rat hippocampal neurons (Takahashi et al., 2012).
claims.evidence: The claim cites a previous study proposing convergent input as an explanation for coordinated spine activity.

claims.claim: In developing hippocampal neurons, an initial Ca++ transient can be propagated to neighboring spines via Ca++ release from intracellular stores.
claims.source: In developing hippocampal neurons, an initial Ca++ transient can be propagated to neighboring spines via Ca++ release from intracellular stores (Lee et al., 2016).
claims.evidence: The claim cites a previous study showing Ca++ propagation in hippocampal neurons.

claims.claim: In hippocampal neurons, local glutamate uncaging triggers ryanodine-insensitive Ca++ transients in the excited spine but this effect is rapid (~250 ms).
claims.source: In hippocampal neurons, local glutamate uncaging triggers ryanodine-insensitive Ca++ transients in the excited spine but this effect is rapid (~250 ms) (Lee et al., 2016) and thus a similar rapid initial Ca++ transient might have been missed by our experimental set up that detects GCaMP signals ~ 2 s after ceChrimson activation (Figure 4K).
claims.evidence: The claim cites a previous study showing rapid Ca++ transients in hippocampal neurons and uses this to interpret the current experimental results.

claims.claim: Spine shape and density are modulated throughout development in mammalian neurons.
claims.source: In mammalian neurons, spine shape and density are modulated throughout development (Fiala et al., 1998; Harris et al., 1992; Kanjhan et al., 2016a).
claims.evidence: The claim cites previous studies showing developmental modulation of spine morphology in mammals.

claims.claim: Dendritic spines can be modulated by changes in synaptic strength.
claims.source: Dendritic spines can be modulated by changes in synaptic strength (Bourne and Harris, 2008; Nimchinsky et al., 2002; Rochefort and Konnerth, 2012).
claims.evidence: The claim cites established knowledge about spine modulation by synaptic strength.

claims.claim: Long-term potentiation is correlated with increased numbers of spines in the mammalian brain.
claims.source: Long-term potentiation is correlated with increased numbers of spines in the mammalian brain (Engert and Bonhoeffer, 1999; Trachtenberg et al., 2002; Holtmaat et al., 2005).
claims.evidence: The claim cites previous studies showing correlation between LTP and spine density.

claims.claim: Hyperactivity is associated with increased dendritic spine density in hypoglossal motor neurons.
claims.source: Similarly, hyperactivity is associated with increased dendritic spine density in hypoglossal motor neurons (Kanjhan et al., 2016b).
claims.evidence: The claim cites a previous study showing activity-dependent spine density changes in motor neurons.

claims.claim: Long-term depression induces spine shrinkage and may lead to spine elimination.
claims.source: Conversely, long-term depression induces spine shrinkage (Zhou et al., 2004) and may lead to their elimination (Hasegawa et al., 2015).
claims.evidence: The claim cites previous studies showing effects of LTD on spine morphology.

claims.claim: The prevalence of postsynaptic protrusions in vertebrate and invertebrate nervous systems suggests that spines are ancient structures.
claims.source: The prevalence of postsynaptic protrusions in vertebrate and invertebrate nervous systems suggests that spines are ancient structures and thus could be effectively investigated in a variety of model organisms (Leiss, 2008; Petralia et al., 2016).
claims.evidence: The claim is an inference based on the widespread presence of spine-like structures across species, with citations to reviews discussing this.

claims.claim: C. elegans is transparent, so live imaging does not require surgery or other invasive methods that are typically necessary for in vivo imaging of spines in an intact mammalian nervous system.
claims.source: Because C. elegans is transparent, live imaging does not require surgery or other invasive methods that are typically necessary for in vivo imaging of spines in an intact mammalian nervous system.
claims.evidence: The claim is based on established knowledge about C. elegans transparency and the requirements for mammalian in vivo imaging.

claims.claim: A recent study reported that neurexin is necessary for spine morphogenesis in DDs, and in this case, neuroligin is not required.
claims.source: A recent study, for example, reported that neurexin, a conserved membrane protein and established regulator of synaptic assembly, is necessary for spine morphogenesis in DDs. Interestingly, in this case, neuroligin, the canonical neurexin ligand, is not required, suggesting a potentially new neurexin-dependent mechanism of synaptogenesis (Oliver et al., 2018; Philbrook et al., 2018).
claims.evidence: The claim cites recent studies showing neurexin's role in DD spine morphogenesis.

claims.claim: Other neurons reported to have 'short branches' in the original EM reconstruction of the adult C. elegans are likely to display bona fide dendritic spines.
claims.source: Thus, other neurons reported to have 'short branches' in the original EM reconstruction of the adult C. elegans (White et al., 1986), the cholinergic (RMD, SMD) and GABAergic (RME) motor neurons and the interneuron (RIP), are likely to display bona fide dendritic spines.
claims.evidence: The claim is an inference based on the current findings and previous EM observations, with citation to the original EM reconstruction.

claims.claim: A developmentally regulated remodeling program transforms presynaptic boutons into postsynaptic spines in larval DD neurons.
claims.source: Finally, a developmentally regulated remodeling program (Kurup and Jin, 2016; Petersen et al., 2011; White et al., 1978) transforms presynaptic boutons into postsynaptic spines in larval DD neurons and thus could be especially useful for live imaging studies of synaptic plasticity and spine morphogenesis.
claims.evidence: The claim cites previous studies describing the DD remodeling program.

claims.claim: In the adult, Dorsal D (DD) class GABAergic motor neurons extend axons to innervate dorsal muscles and receive cholinergic input at ventral dendrites.
claims.source: In the adult, Dorsal D (DD) class GABAergic motor neurons extend axons to innervate dorsal muscles and receive cholinergic input at ventral dendrites (Figure 1A).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by the schematic in Figure 1A showing DD neuron anatomy.

claims.claim: Airyscan imaging is a type of super-resolution microscopy.
claims.source: We used Airyscan imaging, a type of super-resolution microscopy (Korobchevskaya et al., 2017), to detect spine-like projections on the ventral processes of adult DD neurons labeled with a cytosolic mCherry marker (Figure 1B).
claims.evidence: The claim cites a reference describing Airyscan as a super-resolution technique.

claims.claim: LifeAct::GFP is an actin marker.
claims.source: Because the actin cytoskeleton is a structural hallmark of vertebrate dendritic spines (Cingolani and Goda, 2008), we also labeled DD neurons with the actin marker, LifeAct::GFP (Riedl et al., 2008).
claims.evidence: The claim cites the original publication describing LifeAct::GFP as an actin marker.

claims.claim: High Pressure Freezing (HPF) avoids potential artifacts arising from chemical fixation.
claims.source: For this experiment, young adult animals were prepared using High Pressure Freezing (HPF) to avoid potential artifacts arising from chemical fixation (Mulcahy et al., 2018; Weimer et al., 2006; White et al., 1986).
claims.evidence: The claim cites previous studies supporting the use of HPF to avoid fixation artifacts.

claims.claim: The acetylcholine receptor (AChR) subunit ACR-12 is postsynaptic to cholinergic inputs at GABAergic motor neurons.
claims.source: The acetylcholine receptor (AChR) subunit ACR-12 is postsynaptic to cholinergic inputs at GABAergic motor neurons (Petrash et al., 2013), and has been previously shown to localize to DD1 dendritic protrusions (Figure 2E) (He et al., 2015; Philbrook et al., 2018).
claims.evidence: The claim cites previous studies characterizing ACR-12 localization.

claims.claim: NATF (Native and Tissue-Specific Fluorescence) relies on the reconstitution of superfolder GFP (sfGFP) from the split-sfGFP fragments, GFP1-10 and GFP11.
claims.source: NATF (Native and Tissue-Specific Fluorescence) relies on the reconstitution of superfolder GFP (sfGFP) from the split-sfGFP fragments, GFP1-10 and GFP11 (He et al., 2019).
claims.evidence: The claim cites the publication describing the NATF method.

claims.claim: LEV-10 is a co-factor protein of the acetylcholine receptor complex.
claims.source: To obviate the possibility that localization of ACR-12::GFP clusters to DD spines results from over-expression, we used a new live-cell labeling scheme to detect an endogenous component of the acetylcholine receptor complex, the co-factor protein LEV-10 (Gally et al., 2004).
claims.evidence: The claim cites a previous study characterizing LEV-10 as a co-factor of the acetylcholine receptor.

claims.claim: Most C. elegans postsynaptic terminals do not display electron dense postsynaptic densities in electron micrographs.
claims.source: Our EM analysis confirmed that DD spines do not display electron dense postsynaptic densities (PSDs), a feature that is also not detected in electron micrographs of most C. elegans postsynaptic terminals (Lim et al., 2016; White et al., 1976; White et al., 1986; Zhen et al., 2000).
claims.evidence: The claim cites multiple previous EM studies of C. elegans synapses.

claims.claim: Postsynaptic assemblages at non-glutamatergic synapses likely comprise distinct sets of scaffolding proteins, some of which are readily stained by heavy atoms used for EM imaging of glutamatergic synapses.
claims.source: Postsynaptic assemblages at these synapses likely comprise distinct sets of scaffolding proteins, some of which are readily stained by heavy atoms used for EM imaging of glutamatergic synapses (Petralia et al., 2005; Petralia et al., 2016).
claims.evidence: The claim is an inference based on cited studies about postsynaptic protein composition at different synapse types.

claims.claim: The original EM reconstruction of the C. elegans nervous system detected spine-like structures on VD neurons.
claims.source: In the adult C. elegans motor circuit, dendrites of the DD-class GABAergic motor neurons receive cholinergic input in the ventral nerve cord, whereas the VD class receives input in the dorsal nerve cord (Figure 4—figure supplement 1A). Because the original EM reconstruction of the C. elegans nervous system detected spine-like structures on VD neurons (White et al., 1976), we sought to verify this finding by using the LifeAct::GFP marker for Airyscan imaging.
claims.evidence: The claim cites the original EM reconstruction study.

claims.claim: Both the DD and VD classes of ventral cord GABAergic motor neurons display dendritic spines.
claims.source: Thus, both the DD and VD classes of ventral cord GABAergic motor neurons display dendritic spines (White et al., 1976; White et al., 1986).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by the current study's data and cites the original EM reconstruction studies.

claims.claim: Only 10% of excitatory synapses in the mature mammalian cortex are positioned on dendritic processes.
claims.source: This finding parallels the observation that only 10% of excitatory synapses in the mature mammalian cortex are positioned on dendritic processes (Cingolani and Goda, 2008).
claims.evidence: The claim cites a previous study about synapse distribution in mammalian cortex.

claims.claim: The majority of DD1 spines (9/12) are postsynaptic to the same cholinergic motor neuron VA2.
claims.source: For example, the majority of DD1 spines (9/12) are postsynaptic to the same cholinergic motor neuron VA2 (Figure 2C).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by quantitative analysis of EM reconstruction data shown in Figure 2C.

claims.claim: Spines of mammalian cortical neurons can display multiple assemblages of the postsynaptic protein PSD-95.
claims.source: 43.3% of spines (n = 55/127) had more than one ACR-12::GFP cluster (Figure 2H), a finding that mirrors a recent observation that spines of mammalian cortical neurons can display multiple assemblages of the postsynaptic protein PSD-95 (Hruska et al., 2018).
claims.evidence: The claim cites a recent study showing multiple PSD-95 assemblages in mammalian spines.

claims.claim: Six DD motor neurons are located in the C. elegans ventral nerve cord.
claims.source: Six DD motor neurons are located in the C. elegans ventral nerve cord.
claims.evidence: The claim is stated in the figure legend for Figure 1A and represents established anatomical knowledge.

claims.claim: In the adult, DD presynaptic boutons innervate dorsal muscles and DD postsynaptic termini (spines) receive cholinergic input from VA and VB motor neurons on the ventral side.
claims.source: In the adult, DD presynaptic boutons (oblong ovals) innervate dorsal muscles (gray cells) and DD postsynaptic termini (spines) receive cholinergic input from VA and VB motor neurons on the ventral side (magenta).
claims.evidence: The claim is stated in the figure legend for Figure 1A and represents established anatomical knowledge.

claims.claim: Spine density of young adults revealed by mCherry is 3.68 ± 0.8 spines/10 µm.
claims.source: Spine density of young adults revealed by mCherry (3.68 ± 0.8 spines/10 µm) or LifeAct::GFP (3.43 ± 1.2 spines/10 µm) is not significantly different (t test, p=0.0855, n > 16 worms).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by quantitative measurements reported in the text.

claims.claim: Spine density of young adults revealed by LifeAct::GFP is 3.43 ± 1.2 spines/10 µm.
claims.source: Spine density of young adults revealed by mCherry (3.68 ± 0.8 spines/10 µm) or LifeAct::GFP (3.43 ± 1.2 spines/10 µm) is not significantly different (t test, p=0.0855, n > 16 worms).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by quantitative measurements reported in the text.

claims.claim: Adult DD motor neurons have 55.5 ± 14.5% thin/mushroom spines, 10.3 ± 8.70% filopodial spines, 18.8 ± 10.4% stubby spines, and 15.4 ± 6.0% branched spines.
claims.source: LifeAct::GFP reveals 1. Thin/Mushroom (55.5 ± 14.5%), 2. Filopodial (10.3 ± 8.70%), 3. Stubby (18.8 ± 10.4%), 4. Branched spines (15.4 ± 6.0%) in adult DD motor neurons.
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by quantitative classification of spine morphologies from imaging data.

claims.claim: Spine density determined by 3D EM reconstruction of DD1 is 4.2 spines/10 µm.
claims.source: Spine densities determined from young adult DD neurons labeled with mCherry (3.68 ± 0.8 spines/10 µm), LifeAct::GFP (3.43 ± 1.2spines/10 µm) and MYR::mRuby (3.09 ± 0.8 spines/10 µm) are not significantly different and are comparable to spine density determined by 3D EM reconstruction of DD1 (4.2 spines/10 µm) (dashed blue line).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by EM reconstruction data.

claims.claim: Spine density of young adults revealed by MYR::mRuby is 3.09 ± 0.8 spines/10 µm.
claims.source: Spine densities determined from young adult DD neurons labeled with mCherry (3.68 ± 0.8 spines/10 µm), LifeAct::GFP (3.43 ± 1.2spines/10 µm) and MYR::mRuby (3.09 ± 0.8 spines/10 µm) are not significantly different and are comparable to spine density determined by 3D EM reconstruction of DD1 (4.2 spines/10 µm) (dashed blue line).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by quantitative measurements from imaging data.

claims.claim: Wild-type young adults show 3.53 ± 1.0 spines/10 µm vs toca-1(tm2056) with 2.77 ± 1.1 spines/10 µm (t test, p<0.001).
claims.source: WT young adults show 3.53 ± 1.0 spines/10 µm vs toca-1 (tm2056) with 2.77 ± 1.1 spines/10 µm (t test, *** is p<0.001).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by quantitative measurements comparing wild-type and mutant animals.

claims.claim: Spine density is reduced with RNAi of wave/wve-1 (2.24 ± 0.7 spines/10 µm) or p21/arx-5 RNAi (2.20 ± 0.7 spines/10 µm) versus Empty Vector control (2.9 ± 0.4 spines/10 µm).
claims.source: Spine density is reduced with RNAi of wave/wve-1 (2.24 ± 0.7 spines/10 µm) or p21/arx-5 RNAi (2.20 ± 0.7 spines/10 µm) versus Empty Vector (E.V.) control (2.9 ± 0.4 spines/10 µm). One-way ANOVA with Dunnett's multiple comparison test, ** is p<0.01, n > 9 worms.
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by quantitative measurements from RNAi experiments.

claims.claim: TOCA-1a expression in DD neurons rescues the spine density defect in toca-1(tm2056) mutants (3.05 ± 0.8 spines/10 µm).
claims.source: wild-type young adults show 3.53 ± 1.0 spines/10 µm vs 2.35 ± 0.9 spines/10 µm in toca-1(tm2056), which is rescued with TOCA-1a expression in DD neurons (Pflp-13::TOCA-1a::mCherry)=3.05 ± 0.8 spines/10 µm.
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by quantitative measurements from rescue experiments.

claims.claim: 84.1 ± 6.4% of DD spines are contacted by cholinergic presynaptic sites as detected by Airyscan imaging.
claims.source: Frequency of spines contacted by cholinergic presynaptic sites detected by Airyscan imaging (contacted, 84.1 ± 6.4% vs not contacted, 15.8 ± 6.4%, n = 128 spines from seven worms) or by EM (contacted, 100% vs not contacted, 0%, n = 12 spines from one worm).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by quantitative analysis of Airyscan imaging data.

claims.claim: 100% of DD spines are contacted by cholinergic presynaptic sites as detected by EM.
claims.source: Frequency of spines contacted by cholinergic presynaptic sites detected by Airyscan imaging (contacted, 84.1 ± 6.4% vs not contacted, 15.8 ± 6.4%, n = 128 spines from seven worms) or by EM (contacted, 100% vs not contacted, 0%, n = 12 spines from one worm).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by quantitative analysis of EM reconstruction data.

claims.claim: 68.5% of ACR-12::GFP clusters are localized at spine tips.
claims.source: We detected ACR-12::GFP clusters on ~95% of DD spines (n = 121/127) (Figure 2F–G), with 68.5% (n = 87/127) localized at spine tips and the remainder either positioned along the lateral side of the spine (~12%, n = 15/127) or at both the side and tip (~15%, n = 19/127) (Figure 2G).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by quantitative analysis of ACR-12::GFP localization.

claims.claim: Approximately 12% of ACR-12::GFP clusters are positioned along the lateral side of the spine.
claims.source: We detected ACR-12::GFP clusters on ~95% of DD spines (n = 121/127) (Figure 2F–G), with 68.5% (n = 87/127) localized at spine tips and the remainder either positioned along the lateral side of the spine (~12%, n = 15/127) or at both the side and tip (~15%, n = 19/127) (Figure 2G).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by quantitative analysis of ACR-12::GFP localization.

claims.claim: Approximately 15% of ACR-12::GFP clusters are positioned at both the side and tip of spines.
claims.source: We detected ACR-12::GFP clusters on ~95% of DD spines (n = 121/127) (Figure 2F–G), with 68.5% (n = 87/127) localized at spine tips and the remainder either positioned along the lateral side of the spine (~12%, n = 15/127) or at both the side and tip (~15%, n = 19/127) (Figure 2G).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by quantitative analysis of ACR-12::GFP localization.

claims.claim: VD spine density is 3.01 ± 1.43 spines/10 µm as measured by Airyscan imaging.
claims.source: VD spine density (3.01 ± 1.43 spines/10 µm), n = 17.
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by quantitative measurements from Airyscan imaging.

claims.claim: VD2 spine density detected by 3D EM is 3.33 spines/10 µm.
claims.source: Dashed blue line represents spine density detected in VD2 with 3D EM (3.33 spines/10 µm).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by EM reconstruction data.

claims.claim: 50.0% of DA and DB inputs are adjacent to VD spines.
claims.source: 50.0% (n = 11/22) of DA and DB inputs are adjacent to VD spines.
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by quantitative analysis of EM reconstruction data.

claims.claim: DD spine density at the L4 stage is reduced by growth on histamine (2.58 ± 0.6) vs control (3.49 ± 0.9).
claims.source: DD spine density at the L4 stage is reduced by growth on histamine (2.58 ± 0.6) vs control (3.49 ± 0.9). T-test, **=p < 0.01, n > 17.
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by quantitative measurements from histamine treatment experiments.

claims.claim: Exposure to red-light for 6 hr elevates spine density at the L3 stage (3.9 ± 0.8) vs control (2.59 ± 0.8).
claims.source: Exposure to red-light for 6 hr elevates spine density at the L3 stage (3.9 ± 0.8) vs control (2.59 ± 0.8). T-test, *** is p<0.001, n > 10.
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by quantitative measurements from optogenetic activation experiments.

results.result: C. elegans DD motor neuron dendritic spines are structurally defined by a dynamic actin cytoskeleton that is enriched in spines compared to dendritic shafts, and actin regulators including the Arp2/3 complex, TOCA-1, and Wave Regulatory Complex are required cell-autonomously to maintain spine density.
results.evaluation: Claims C1, C6, C12, C13, and C14 collectively demonstrate that DD spines contain enriched actin (quantified by LifeAct::GFP spine/shaft ratio >1 with p<0.0001), show dynamic actin remodeling in live imaging, and require actin polymerization machinery for formation. The genetic rescue experiment (C14) confirms cell-autonomous function. The data converge from multiple independent approaches (super-resolution imaging, live imaging, genetics).

results.result: DD motor neurons display multiple morphological classes of dendritic spines (predominantly thin/mushroom at 55.5±14.5%, with lesser fractions of filopodial, stubby, and branched forms) that can undergo dynamic remodeling in vivo.
results.evaluation: Claims C8, C9, C10, C11, and C94 are supported by quantitative morphological classification from both Airyscan imaging and EM reconstruction showing consistent spine type distributions. Live imaging directly demonstrates spine remodeling and transient filopodial extensions (11/25 movies), providing direct evidence of structural plasticity.

results.result: DD dendritic spines directly appose presynaptic cholinergic motor neuron terminals, with approximately 84% of spines contacted by at least one presynaptic cluster and 40% receiving input from multiple presynaptic terminals.
results.evaluation: Claims C2, C15-C19 are supported by convergent evidence from Airyscan imaging (84.1±6.4% of spines contacted) and EM reconstruction (100% of 12 DD1 spines in direct apposition with VA/VB terminals, with 84.8% of cholinergic inputs apposing spines). The quantitative agreement between independent methods strengthens the conclusion.

results.result: Postsynaptic acetylcholine receptor components (ACR-12 and LEV-10) localize to DD spines, with ACR-12::GFP detected on ~95% of spines and endogenous LEV-10 detected at 100% of spines using NATF labeling.
results.evaluation: Claims C20-C22 are supported by quantitative Airyscan imaging showing ACR-12::GFP on 95% of spines (121/127) and NATF labeling detecting endogenous LEV-10 at 100% of spines (159/159). The NATF approach addresses potential overexpression artifacts from the ACR-12::GFP transgene, strengthening the conclusion that these are functional postsynaptic sites.

results.result: DD dendritic spines contain smooth endoplasmic reticulum (SER)-like structures and ribosomes (detected in ~44.5% of spines by RPS-18::GFP), but lack mitochondria and microtubules.
results.evaluation: Claims C3, C24-C26 are supported by EM reconstruction detecting SER-like cisternae and apparent ribosomes in DD1 spines, corroborated by light microscopy detecting RPS-18::GFP in 44.5±12.0% of spines. However, the authors appropriately note that conclusions about mitochondria and microtubules should be interpreted cautiously given the small sample (n=12 spines from one animal).

results.result: DD spines display spontaneous calcium transients lasting several seconds, with adjacent spines showing coordinated Ca++ activity (~50% simultaneous transients), and optogenetic activation of presynaptic VA neurons triggers correlated GCaMP6s fluorescence in DD spines.
results.evaluation: Claims C4, C27-C30 are supported by GCaMP6s live imaging showing spontaneous Ca++ transients and statistical analysis demonstrating non-random coordination between adjacent spines (KS test, p<0.0001). Optogenetic experiments show correlation between ceChrimson activation and GCaMP6s signals, with appropriate controls (EtOH vs ATR). The data support functional Ca++ signaling in spines.

results.result: Local cholinergic release can trigger Ca++ changes that propagate to neighboring and distant spines via ryanodine receptor-dependent Ca++ release from intracellular stores.
results.evaluation: Claims C31-C33 are supported by local optogenetic activation experiments showing Ca++ propagation to adjacent and distant spines, pharmacological blockade with ryanodine substantially attenuating Ca++ transients, and genetic evidence from unc-68 mutants showing reduced intrinsic Ca++ dynamics. The convergence of pharmacological and genetic approaches strengthens the mechanistic conclusion.

results.result: DD spine density is regulated by cholinergic activity in a developmentally dynamic manner, with reduced acetylcholine signaling decreasing spine density and increased acetylcholine levels or optogenetic activation of cholinergic neurons increasing spine density.
results.evaluation: Claims C5, C34-C39 are supported by multiple complementary approaches: developmental time course showing increasing spine density (C34), genetic manipulations of acetylcholine levels (unc-17 mutants showing reduced density, ace-1;ace-2 mutants showing precocious elevation), acute pharmacological silencing with histamine, and optogenetic activation experiments. The convergence of genetic, pharmacological, and optogenetic evidence strongly supports activity-dependent regulation.

results.result: VD-class GABAergic motor neurons also display dendritic spines throughout the dorsal nerve cord, with EM reconstruction detecting nine spines in 27 μm of VD2 dendrite that are juxtaposed to presynaptic cholinergic motor neuron termini.
results.evaluation: Claims C40-C42 and C86 are supported by Airyscan imaging after DD ablation confirming VD spines and EM reconstruction showing nine VD2 spines with similar characteristics to DD spines (apposition to cholinergic terminals). This extends the main findings to a second class of GABAergic motor neurons, demonstrating generalizability.

results.result: Spine density measurements are consistent across multiple labeling methods (cytoplasmic mCherry: 3.68±0.8, LifeAct::GFP: 3.43±1.2, MYR::mRuby: 3.09±0.8 spines/10 μm) and comparable to EM reconstruction (4.2 spines/10 μm).
results.evaluation: Claims C7, C92-C93, C95-C96 demonstrate methodological consistency with no significant differences between markers (t-test, p=0.0855) and good agreement with EM reconstruction. This validates the imaging approaches and suggests that marker overexpression does not substantially alter spine density.

results.result: DD spines do not display electron-dense postsynaptic densities (PSDs), consistent with most C. elegans postsynaptic terminals and non-glutamatergic synapses in vertebrates.
results.evaluation: Claims C23 and C83 are supported by EM analysis and appropriately contextualized with citations to previous C. elegans studies and vertebrate non-glutamatergic synapses. The absence of PSDs does not contradict the functional nature of these spines, as PSDs are not universal features of all synapse types.

results.result: Prior work has established that dendritic spines were originally described by Ramon y Cajal, are regulated by neural activity and correlated with learning/memory, and spine-like structures have been reported in invertebrates including C. elegans and Ascaris.
results.evaluation: Claims C43-C48 accurately cite and summarize prior literature establishing the historical context and previous observations of spine-like structures in nematodes. The citations appear appropriate and the claims are consistent with established knowledge in the field.

results.result: The structural and functional features of C. elegans DD spines parallel those described for mammalian dendritic spines, including actin enrichment, morphological heterogeneity attributed to active remodeling, and dependence on Arp2/3 complex function.
results.evaluation: Claims C49-C53 appropriately cite mammalian literature to contextualize the C. elegans findings. The parallels drawn are supported by the experimental data in the current study and the citations appear accurate. This establishes the relevance of C. elegans spines as a model for understanding conserved spine biology.

results.result: Prior work has established that functional dendritic spines are sites of presynaptic input, can receive multiple inputs, contain SER and ribosomes, and typically lack mitochondria and microtubules in mature neurons.
results.evaluation: Claims C54-C60 accurately cite and summarize established knowledge about mammalian dendritic spine ultrastructure and function. The citations appear appropriate and provide context for interpreting the C. elegans findings. The comparison to non-glutamatergic vertebrate synapses (C56) is particularly relevant given the cholinergic nature of DD spine inputs.

results.result: Prior work has established that Ca++ is a key signaling molecule for synaptic plasticity, and mechanisms of Ca++ propagation between spines via intracellular stores have been described in mammalian neurons.
results.evaluation: Claims C61-C65 appropriately cite prior literature on Ca++ signaling in synaptic plasticity and Ca++ propagation mechanisms. Claim C65 thoughtfully acknowledges a potential limitation of the current study (2 s temporal resolution) in detecting rapid initial Ca++ transients observed in mammalian systems (~250 ms).

results.result: Prior work has established that mammalian spine density and morphology are modulated during development and by changes in synaptic strength, with LTP correlated with increased spine numbers and LTD inducing spine shrinkage.
results.evaluation: Claims C66-C70 accurately cite established literature on activity-dependent regulation of mammalian spine density and morphology. These citations provide appropriate context for the activity-dependent regulation observed in C. elegans DD spines.

results.result: The prevalence of spine-like structures across species suggests they are ancient structures, and C. elegans offers experimental advantages including transparency for live imaging and genetic tractability, with other C. elegans neurons likely displaying bona fide dendritic spines.
results.evaluation: Claims C71-C75 present reasonable inferences about the evolutionary conservation of spines and the advantages of C. elegans as a model system. The inference that other C. elegans neurons with 'short branches' likely have spines (C74) is appropriately qualified as 'likely' and supported by the current findings. The citations to prior work on DD remodeling (C75) and neurexin function (C73) are appropriate.

results.result: The study employed appropriate methods including Airyscan super-resolution microscopy, LifeAct::GFP as an actin marker, high-pressure freezing for EM to avoid fixation artifacts, and NATF labeling to detect endogenous proteins.
results.evaluation: Claims C76-C82 describe methodological approaches with appropriate citations. The use of HPF for EM (C79) is well-justified to avoid chemical fixation artifacts. The NATF method (C81-C82) is appropriately cited and addresses potential overexpression artifacts. These methodological details support the rigor of the experimental approaches.

results.result: Genetic disruption of actin regulators reduces DD spine density (toca-1 mutants: 2.77±1.1 vs WT: 3.53±1.0 spines/10 μm; wave-1 RNAi: 2.24±0.7; arx-5 RNAi: 2.20±0.7 vs control: 2.9±0.4), with DD-specific TOCA-1 expression rescuing the defect (3.05±0.8 spines/10 μm).
results.evaluation: Claims C97-C99 present quantitative data with appropriate statistical tests (t-test for C97, ANOVA with Dunnett's test for C98) showing significant reductions in spine density upon disruption of actin regulators. The rescue experiment (C99) demonstrates cell-autonomous function and specificity of the phenotype.

results.result: Quantitative analysis shows that 84.1±6.4% of DD spines are contacted by cholinergic presynaptic sites by Airyscan imaging (100% by EM), with ACR-12::GFP clusters localized predominantly at spine tips (68.5%) with lesser fractions along the spine side (12%) or at both locations (15%).
results.evaluation: Claims C100-C104 present detailed quantitative data on spine-synapse apposition and receptor localization. The agreement between Airyscan (84.1%) and EM (100%) methods is reasonable given the different sample sizes and detection limits. The subcellular localization data for ACR-12::GFP provides important detail about receptor organization.

results.result: VD spine density measured by Airyscan imaging (3.01±1.43 spines/10 μm) is comparable to EM reconstruction (3.33 spines/10 μm), with 50% of DA and DB cholinergic inputs adjacent to VD spines.
results.evaluation: Claims C105-C107 present quantitative data for VD neurons showing consistency between imaging methods and demonstrating that VD spines share key features with DD spines. The lower percentage of inputs apposing VD spines (50%) compared to DD spines (84.8%) is an interesting difference that could reflect biological variation or technical factors.

results.result: Acute manipulation of cholinergic activity during development affects spine density, with histamine-mediated silencing reducing density at L4 (2.58±0.6 vs control 3.49±0.9) and optogenetic activation increasing density at L3 (3.9±0.8 vs control 2.59±0.8).
results.evaluation: Claims C108-C109 present quantitative data from temporal manipulation experiments with appropriate statistical tests (t-tests with p<0.01 and p<0.001). These experiments complement the genetic manipulations and demonstrate that activity-dependent regulation can occur on developmental timescales.

results.result: Contextual claims about postsynaptic protein composition at different synapse types, prior EM observations of VD spines, synapse distribution in mammalian cortex, convergent input to DD1 spines from VA2, and anatomical features of DD neurons.
results.evaluation: Claims C84-C91 include a mix of inferences based on cited literature (C84, C87, C89), citations to prior work (C85), and specific quantitative observations from the current study (C88). Claim C84 is appropriately qualified as 'likely' and supported by citations. The anatomical descriptions (C90-C91) represent established knowledge.
